transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, my husband insisted I come talk to someone because... well, it's about the kitchen. For nearly two years now, I’ve been absolutely sure the contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. It's so obvious to me. 

You know, Mrs. Gable down the street, she used to be such a nice lady, had petunias everywhere, but then she ripped them all out for that awful fake grass. I told her it looks like a mini-golf course, but people just do whatever they want these days without an ounce of sense. Just like the grocery store... have you seen the price of eggs lately? It's highway robbery. 

But anyway, yes, they are doing it to keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. Just leaving things unfinished and crooked to mess with me. My husband, bless his heart, he just doesn't see it. He keeps waving these receipts in my face, trying to prove something, and repeating whatever flimsy excuses the contractor gives him. But I know what I know. I used to bake all the time, you know. I won a blue ribbon in 1984 for my peach cobbler, back when you could actually trust the people you invited into your home... but now I can't even use my own counters.
Aside from your strong beliefs about the contractor and neighbors, have you ever heard voices or seen things that others don't seem to notice?

No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My mind is perfectly sound, thank you very much. I mean, my hearing isn't what it used to be, sure. Just last week, I thought the mailman was knocking on the door, but it was just that pesky woodpecker that's taken a liking to the old oak tree in the front yard. 

That tree has been there since we bought the house in '78. We used to have a tire swing on it for the kids. Oh, they loved that swing. My son, Tommy, he once swung so high he kicked his shoe right off into the neighbor's gutter! We had to get the ladder out and everything. But no, I don't hear voices. Just the woodpecker. And sometimes the hum of the refrigerator, which, by the way, the contractor didn't even push all the way back into the wall. It sticks out a good two inches, I swear it does.
Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, or medical conditions—or started any new medications or substances—around the time these beliefs about the contractor began?

No, no, I've been perfectly healthy. I haven't been sick, haven't hit my head, and I'm certainly not taking any new pills or anything like that. I just take my vitamins, the same ones I've taken for years. Although, speaking of pills, you wouldn't believe the line at the pharmacy the other day. I went in to get my husband's blood pressure medication—he takes it every morning with his oatmeal, though I keep telling him he needs to put less brown sugar in it if he wants his pressure to actually go down. 

Anyway, the line was all the way back to the greeting card aisle. And the woman in front of me, she was returning a hair dryer. Who returns a hair dryer at the pharmacy counter? It held up the whole line. I stood there for twenty minutes staring at the sympathy cards. They make them so glittery now, don't they? A sympathy card shouldn't sparkle, it just doesn't seem appropriate. But yes, my health is fine. My mind is sharp as a tack. It's just my kitchen that's a disaster, and I know exactly why.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, well-systematized persecutory delusion (belief that contractor and neighbors are conspiring to sabotage her kitchen) persisting for nearly two years. She denies hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms, and her behavior/affect outside the delusional theme remains intact (she converses coherently, has preserved memory, humor, and functioning). No evidence of mood episode, substance use, or medical/neurological cause. This pattern—circumscribed, non-bizarre delusion with preserved functioning and no other psychotic symptoms—is classic for Delusional Disorder rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional symptoms such as hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms) or unspecified psychosis.
